repudiate

rih-PYOO-dee-ayt · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To repudiate is to formally reject or disown something, often as false or unacceptable.

After decades of silence, the aging author finally repudiated the offensive views expressed in his early novels.

Example

When evidence surfaced that the charity's founder had misused donations, the board publicly repudiated him and cut all remaining ties.

To repudiate someone or something is to formally and firmly reject it, often to distance yourself from something shameful or false.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

disown: To disown is to refuse to accept something -- or someone -- as your own: parents disown a child, an artist disowns an early work. To repudiate reaches wider: you can repudiate anything you find false or shameful, whether or not it was ever yours, and the rejection is formal and public.

reject: To reject is the everyday word for refusing to accept or believe something -- a plan, an excuse, an offer. To repudiate is its formal, public cousin: a firm denunciation of a claim, belief, debt, or tie, far too strong for ordinary disagreement.

disavow: To disavow is to deny that something is yours or speaks for you -- a campaign disavows a supporter's ugly remarks. To repudiate goes further: beyond denying any connection, it formally condemns the thing itself as false or unacceptable and cuts every tie to it.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

endorse: to publicly express approval or support

embrace: to accept something readily and enthusiastically

Where it sits · how formally and completely it is denied — doubt → repudiate → renounce

doubt vs. repudiate: To doubt something is only to feel mild uncertainty about it -- a doubter is still weighing the claim, while to repudiate it is to cast it out formally and completely.

renounce vs. repudiate: To renounce is to formally give up your own claim, title, or belief -- one step beyond repudiate, which rejects someone else's claim rather than surrendering something of your own.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — re-

prefix — re-: back, away (Latin)

root — pudi-

root — pudi-: to cast off (from Latin repudium, an ancient legal term for a formal divorce)

suffix — -ate

suffix — -ate: forms a verb (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Repudiate is built from re- ('back, away') + pudi- ('to cast off,' from Latin repudium, an ancient legal term for a formal divorce announcement) + -ate (a verb ending). Its deeper root is debated by scholars, so there's no common modern English word to quiz you on here -- just this one fascinating historical cousin.

Use the root in a new word: repudium

Use the root in a new word: repudium: In ancient Rome, a husband could end a marriage simply by declaring a repudium in front of witnesses.

Strength Check

Word Choice

Repudiate is a strong, formal word -- reserve it for firmly and publicly rejecting a claim, belief, debt, or relationship, not for everyday disagreement. It's a closer relative of renege (breaking a personal promise) and rescind (officially cancelling a law, contract, or policy) than it might first appear -- all three describe 'going back' on something, just at different levels of formality.
